{"kind":"proof","text":"Let \(G\) and \(H\) be arbitrary nonabelian groups of order \(21\). We show that they are isomorphic.

For \(G\), Sylow’s theorems give
\[
n_7\mid 3,\qquad n_7\equiv1\pmod 7,
\]
so \(n_7=1\). Thus the subgroup \(N=\langle b\rangle\) of order \(7\) is normal. By Cauchy’s theorem, choose \(a\in G\) of order \(3\). Since \(N\cap\langle a\rangle=\{e\}\), the product \(N\langle a\rangle\) has order \(21\), hence equals \(G\). Therefore every element of \(G\) has a unique expression \(b^s a^r\), where \(0\le s<7\) and \(0\le r<3\).

Because \(N\) is normal, conjugation by \(a\) induces an automorphism of \(N\), so
\[
aba^{-1}=b^i
\]
for some \(i\in\{1,\ldots,6\}\). Since \(a^3=e\), applying conjugation three times gives \(b=b^{i^3}\), and hence
\[
i^3\equiv1\pmod 7.
\]
The solutions are \(i\equiv1,2,4\pmod7\). If \(i=1\), then \(a\) commutes with \(b\); since \(a,b\) generate \(G\), this would make \(G\) abelian. Thus \(i=2\) or \(i=4\). If \(i=4\), replace \(a\) by \(a^{-1}\); conjugation by \(a^{-1}\) then has exponent \(4^{-1}\equiv2\pmod7\). Consequently, generators \(x,y\) of orders \(3,7\), respectively, may be chosen so that
\[
xyx^{-1}=y^2.
\]

Applying the same argument to \(H\), choose generators \(u,v\) of orders \(3,7\) satisfying
\[
uvu^{-1}=v^2,
\]
and every element of \(H\) is uniquely \(v^s u^r\).

Define
\[
\phi:G\to H,\qquad \phi(y^s x^r)=v^s u^r
\]
for \(0\le s<7\) and \(0\le r<3\). Uniqueness of the normal forms makes \(\phi\) well-defined and bijective. Moreover,
\[
(y^s x^r)(y^q x^t)=y^{s+2^r q}x^{r+t},
\]
with exponents reduced modulo \(7\) and \(3\), respectively. The identical multiplication formula holds for \(v^s u^r\). Hence
\[
\phi\bigl((y^s x^r)(y^q x^t)\bigr)
=v^{s+2^r q}u^{r+t}
=\phi(y^s x^r)\phi(y^q x^t).
\]
Thus \(\phi\) is a bijective homomorphism, so \(G\cong H\). Therefore any two nonabelian groups of order \(21\) are isomorphic.","reason":"The supplied proof’s proposed map is not well-defined merely because generators have matching orders, and its conjugation calculation is incorrect. The repaired proof establishes unique normal forms, normalizes both conjugation actions to exponent \(2\), and verifies the homomorphism using the resulting multiplication formula."}

{"problem": {"theorem": "Prove that any two nonabelian groups of order 21 are isomorphic.", "assumptions": [], "domain": "abstract_algebra", "proof_text": "\begin{proof}

    By Cauchy's theorem we have that if $G$ is a group of order 21 then it has an element $a$ of order 3 and an element $b$ of order 7. By exercise 2.5.41 we have that the subgroup generated by $b$ is normal, so there is some $i=0,1,2,3,4,5,6$ such that $a b a^{-1}=b^i$. We know $i \neq$ 0 since that implies $a b=a$ and so that $b=e$, a contradiction, and we know $i \neq 1$ since then $a b=b a$ and this would imply $G$ is abelian, which we are assuming is not the case.

Now, $a$ has order 3 so we must have $b=a^3 b a^{-3}=b^{i^3}$ mod 7 , and so $i$ is restricted by the modular equation $i^3 \equiv 1 \bmod 7$

\begin{center}

\begin{tabular}{|c|c|}

\hline$x$ & $x^3 \bmod 7$ \\

\hline 2 & 1 \\

\hline 3 & 6 \\

\hline 4 & 1 \\

\hline 5 & 6 \\

\hline 6 & 6 \\

\hline

\end{tabular}

\end{center}

Therefore the only options are $i=2$ and $i=4$. Now suppose $G$ is such that $a b a^{-1}=b^2$ and let $G^{\prime}$ be another group of order 21 with an element $c$ of order 3 and an element $d$ of order 7 such that $c d c^{-1}=d^4$. We now prove that $G$ and $G^{\prime}$ are isomorphic. Define

$$

\begin{aligned}

\phi: G & \rightarrow G^{\prime} \\

a & \mapsto c^{-1} \\

b & \mapsto d

\end{aligned}

$$

since $a$ and $c^{-1}$ have the same order and $b$ and $d$ have the same order this is a well defined function. Since

$$

\begin{aligned}

\phi(a) \phi(b) \phi(a)^{-1} & =c^{-1} d c \\

& =\left(c d^{-1} c^{-1}\right)^{-1} \\

& =\left(d^{-4}\right)^{-1} \\

& =d^4 \\

& =\left(d^2\right)^2 \\

& =\phi(b)^2

\end{aligned}

$$

$\phi$ is actually a homomorphism. For any $c^i d^j \in G^{\prime}$ we have $\phi\left(a^{-i} b^j\right)=c^i d^j$ so $\phi$ is onto and $\phi\left(a^i b^j\right)=c^{-i} d^j=e$ only if $i=j=0$, so $\phi$ is 1-to-l. Therefore $G$ and $G^{\prime}$ are isomorphic and so up to isomorphism there is only one nonabelian group of order 21 .

\end{proof}", "explicit_subgoals": []}, "rule_candidates": [{"id": "grp_first_iso", "name": "First isomorphism theorem for groups", "statement": "If phi: G -> H is a group homomorphism, then G/ker(phi) is isomorphic to im(phi).", "conditions": ["phi is a group homomorphism", "ker(phi) is the kernel of phi"], "conclusion": "G/ker(phi) is isomorphic to im(phi).", "rule_digest": "335c687d26f64e41584f1b8bc575aec9d78223b01c4821bf0056bf8533de0c19", "applicability": "unchecked"}, {"id": "grp_normal_quotient", "name": "Quotient group criterion", "statement": "If N is a normal subgroup of G, then the set of left cosets G/N forms a group under (aN)(bN) = abN.", "conditions": ["N is a subgroup of G", "N is normal in G"], "conclusion": "G/N is a group and coset multiplication is well-defined.", "rule_digest": "f6d458aa2e7463efeea7a535cdbe0f0f7930259cfe7f845b5350ec03454da876", "applicability": "unchecked"}, {"id": "ring_quotient_ideal", "name": "Quotient ring criterion", "statement": "If I is a two-sided ideal of a ring R, then R/I is a quotient ring with operations defined on cosets.", "conditions": ["I is a two-sided ideal of R"], "conclusion": "R/I is a ring and coset operations are well-defined.", "rule_digest": "5c419f063bbc02eba57c0943d5ecce5f2e4c1b370cbb5ad6d69c2e08c3b21835", "applicability": "unchecked"}]}
